descripcion: Idioms are the part of vocabulary with the worst ratio of effort to usefulness, because most course books teach the wrong ones. *It's raining cats and dogs* appears in every textbook and almost nobody says it. This week uses only idioms of middle frequency — the kind that actually appear in conversation between adults — and the rule for using them matters as much as the list: **one per paragraph, never two together.**

filas: to be a waste of time
to cut a long story short
to be in the same boat

ejemplos.texto: *I spent three weeks going round in circles with them.*
*To cut a long story short, they sent me to a different office.*
*There's a lot of red tape, but we're all in the same boat.*
*Sooner or later they'll have to answer.*
*I only did it as a last resort.*

notas: Idioms are almost never changed. Wordplay with them sounds like an error when a learner does it.
Check the register before using one: *to be a pain* is fine with a colleague and wrong in a letter to an office.
Using three in a paragraph sounds like a language course, not a person. One is plenty.

contraste.es: The images are different: Spanish idioms often use the body and animals, English ones often use weather, boats and money. Translating directly almost never works — *no tener pelos en la lengua* has no English version with hair in it.
contraste.de: Some Germanic idioms match English closely (der Apfel fällt nicht weit vom Stamm), others use a different image (es regnet in Strömen – it's raining cats and dogs). Each idiom is best learned as a unit.
contraste.it: Idiom images rarely match: piove a catinelle (basins) is it's raining cats and dogs. Literal translation almost never works, so each idiom is best learned as a unit.
contraste.fr: Idiom images rarely match: il pleut des cordes (ropes) is it's raining cats and dogs. Literal translation almost never works, so each idiom is best learned as a unit.
contraste.pt: Idiom images rarely match: chove a cântaros (jugs) is it's raining cats and dogs. Literal translation almost never works, so each idiom is best learned as a unit.

errores: Translating an idiom from your own language word for word.
Using an informal idiom in a formal text.
Changing the wording: it is *in the same boat*, not *in the same ship*.

es: *ser pan comido* rendered as *be eaten bread* instead of *be a piece of cake*.
de: *Das ist nicht mein Bier* rendered as *That's not my beer* instead of *That's not my problem*.
it: *In bocca al lupo* rendered as *In the mouth of the wolf* instead of *Good luck* or *Break a leg*.
fr: *poser un lapin* rendered as *put a rabbit* instead of *stand someone up*.
pt: *pagar o pato* rendered as *pay the duck* instead of *take the rap* or *carry the can*.

traducciones.pt: o serviço de apoio ao cliente

redemittel.expresion: to cut a long story short
to be in the same boat

mision.consigna: Tell the story of a bureaucratic process you had to go through.
requisitos: from at least two registers; and none translated from Spanish

microtareas.texto: Collect three idioms you actually heard or read this week. Just collect them.
Sort eight idioms into informal, neutral and formal.
Record 90 seconds about a form you had to fill in. Three idioms, no more.

autochequeo: At most one idiom per paragraph?
Does each one fit the register of the text?
Is any one of them a literal translation from Spanish?
Did I change the wording of any fixed expression?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on the idioms. (1) Mark each one and check the wording and the register. (2) Flag any that sound like a literal translation from Spanish. (3) Flag any paragraph with more than one. (4) Give me three idioms an English speaker would have used here. Do not correct anything else.
